question: Before taking an acknowledgment, a New York notary must:

options.text: Know or have satisfactory evidence that the person is the one described in and who executed the instrument
options.why: Correct. Real Property Law §303 states this requirement for every acknowledgment.

options.text: Verify the person's employment
options.why: Wrong. Employment has nothing to do with identity.

options.text: Confirm the person owns the property
options.why: Wrong. Notaries don't verify ownership or title.

options.text: Collect a copy of the person's tax return
options.why: Wrong. Tax documents aren't used for identification.

explanation: No acknowledgment may be taken unless the officer knows or has satisfactory evidence that the person making it is the person described in and who executed the instrument.

refs.title: N.Y. Real Prop. Law §303 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 11)

question: Which is the best form of satisfactory evidence for an unknown signer?

options.text: A current government-issued photo ID with a signature, such as a driver's license or passport
options.why: Correct. A government photo ID lets the notary match the face and signature to a reliable record.

options.text: A business card
options.why: Wrong. Anyone can print a business card.

options.text: A utility bill
options.why: Wrong. A bill has no photo and proves an address at most.

options.text: The signer's own statement of who they are
options.why: Wrong. A signer's word is exactly what identification is meant to test.

explanation: Government-issued photo identification is the standard way to obtain satisfactory evidence of identity.

question: What does 'personal appearance' mean for a traditional New York notarization?

options.text: The signer is physically present before the notary at the time of the act
options.why: Correct. For traditional acts the signer must be in the notary's physical presence.

options.text: The signer calls the notary to confirm the signature
options.why: Wrong. A phone call isn't appearance.

options.text: The signer sends a video message
options.why: Wrong. Only a registered electronic notary using approved communication technology may act remotely.

options.text: The signer's agent appears with the document
options.why: Wrong. Someone else appearing doesn't count as the signer's appearance.

explanation: For traditional notarial acts, the person must appear in person before the notary.
source: 19 NYCRR §182.3(a)(3); NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Professional Conduct)

question: A signer offers an expired driver's license and nothing else. The notary does not know them. The notary should:

options.text: Decline unless the signer can produce other satisfactory evidence
options.why: Correct. If the notary can't be satisfied about identity, the act shouldn't proceed.

options.text: Accept it, since expiration doesn't change a face
options.why: Wrong. An expired ID is weaker evidence, and the notary must be truly satisfied.

options.text: Accept it if the signer pays more
options.why: Wrong. Fees can't buy identification, and New York fees are fixed by law.

options.text: Accept it and write 'expired ID' on the certificate
options.why: Wrong. A note doesn't turn doubtful evidence into satisfactory evidence.

explanation: The notary must be satisfied of identity. An expired card alone may not give that assurance; the notary should seek better evidence or decline.

question: Is a notary's personal knowledge of a signer acceptable in New York?

options.text: Yes, if the notary truly knows the person well enough to be certain of their identity
options.why: Correct. 'Knows' in RPL §303 covers genuine personal knowledge.

options.text: No, ID is always required
options.why: Wrong. The statute allows the officer to 'know' the person.

options.text: Only for relatives
options.why: Wrong. Personal knowledge isn't limited to family.

options.text: Only for affidavits
options.why: Wrong. Personal knowledge works for acknowledgments too.

explanation: A notary may rely on personal knowledge when they actually know the person; otherwise satisfactory evidence is required.

question: Proof of a deed is being made by a subscribing witness. The notary does not know the witness. What must the notary establish?

options.text: The witness's identity, by personal knowledge or satisfactory evidence
options.why: Correct. The subscribing witness is the person appearing and swearing, so the witness must be identified.

options.text: Only the grantor's identity
options.why: Wrong. The grantor isn't present; that's why a subscribing witness is used.

options.text: Nothing, because the witness signed the deed
options.why: Wrong. A signature on the deed doesn't prove who the witness is.

options.text: The witness's citizenship
options.why: Wrong. Citizenship isn't part of identification.

explanation: When an instrument is proved by a subscribing witness, the officer must know or have satisfactory evidence of the witness's identity.

refs.title: N.Y. Real Prop. Law §304 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 11)

question: Why does a notary identify signers?

options.text: To prevent impostors from signing in someone else's name
options.why: Correct. Identity verification is the notary's main safeguard against fraud.

options.text: To check the signer's immigration status
options.why: Wrong. Immigration status isn't part of a notary's duty.

options.text: To confirm the document's legal effect
options.why: Wrong. Legal effect is a question for lawyers.

options.text: To collect marketing data
options.why: Wrong. That would misuse personal information.

explanation: The notary's identification duty exists to prevent fraud and impersonation.

question: A signer's ID shows a different name from the one on the document, with no explanation. The notary should:

options.text: Not proceed until the discrepancy is resolved with satisfactory evidence
options.why: Correct. The notary must be satisfied that the person is the one named in the document.

options.text: Proceed using the name on the document
options.why: Wrong. That certifies an identity the ID doesn't support.

options.text: Proceed using the name on the ID and cross out the document's name
options.why: Wrong. Notaries never change document contents.

options.text: Proceed and attach a photocopy of the ID
options.why: Wrong. A copy doesn't explain the mismatch.

explanation: If the evidence doesn't match the person named in the document, the notary isn't satisfied of identity and should not act.

question: For an electronic notarial act, the notary does not personally know the remote signer. Which method satisfies identity under New York rules?

options.text: Credential analysis of a government ID plus identity proofing
options.why: Correct. Remote signers who aren't personally known must pass both credential analysis and identity proofing.

options.text: The signer holding their ID up to a phone camera only
options.why: Wrong. A visual check alone doesn't meet the credential-analysis and identity-proofing requirements.

options.text: An emailed scan of a passport
options.why: Wrong. A scan can't be validated in real time.

options.text: A signed statement from the signer's employer
options.why: Wrong. That isn't an approved remote identification method.

explanation: New York's electronic notarization rules require credential analysis and identity proofing when the notary lacks personal knowledge of the remote signer.

question: A person arrives with a photocopy of their passport. Is that satisfactory evidence?

options.text: No; the notary should examine an original identification document
options.why: Correct. Copies are easy to alter and can't be checked for security features.

options.text: Yes, if it is in color
options.why: Wrong. A color copy is still a copy.

options.text: Yes, if it is notarized
options.why: Wrong. New York notaries can't certify copies, and a notarized copy wouldn't prove identity anyway.

options.text: Yes, for documents under five pages
options.why: Wrong. Length has no bearing on identification.

explanation: A notary should examine an original ID, not a copy, to be satisfied of identity.

refs.title: 19 NYCRR §182.5 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 17)

question: Should a New York notary notarize the signature of a person who is not present?

options.text: No, never
options.why: Correct. Notarizing for an absent person is a serious violation and can be a crime.

options.text: Yes, if the person is a family member
options.why: Wrong. No family exception exists.

options.text: Yes, if the signature looks familiar
options.why: Wrong. Recognizing a signature isn't personal appearance.

options.text: Yes, if the employer asks
options.why: Wrong. Employers can't waive the appearance requirement.

explanation: The signer must appear before the notary. Notarizing for an absent person creates a false certificate.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Professional Conduct); N.Y. Exec. Law §135-a

question: An elderly signer has no ID, but the notary's long-time neighbor, whom the notary knows well, says she has known the signer for years. What should the notary consider?

options.text: Whether the neighbor's sworn statement, together with any other evidence, truly satisfies the notary of the signer's identity
options.why: Correct. New York uses a 'satisfactory evidence' standard, so the notary must weigh whether the evidence actually removes doubt. A sworn identifying witness known to the notary can help.

options.text: Proceed automatically, since any adult's word is enough
options.why: Wrong. Nothing is automatic; the notary must actually be satisfied.

options.text: Refuse automatically, since ID is always required
options.why: Wrong. New York law speaks of knowledge or satisfactory evidence, not ID only.

options.text: Ask the neighbor to sign the document as the signer
options.why: Wrong. That would be forgery.

explanation: New York's standard is the notary's knowledge or satisfactory evidence. A credible identifying witness under oath can contribute, but the notary must actually be satisfied.

question: A notary records how they identified each signer even though traditional journals are not mandated by statute. Why is that wise?

options.text: It is evidence that the notary used reasonable care if the notarization is later challenged
options.why: Correct. Records protect the notary and the public when a signature is disputed.

options.text: It allows the notary to charge an extra records fee
options.why: Wrong. Fees are fixed by statute.

options.text: It replaces the need to see the signer
options.why: Wrong. Nothing replaces personal appearance.

options.text: It is required for the county clerk's monthly report
options.why: Wrong. No such report exists.

explanation: Recording the identification method is good practice that shows reasonable care.

refs.title: 19 NYCRR §182.9 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 18)

question: Which identification document is generally acceptable?

options.text: A U.S. passport
options.why: Correct. It is government-issued with a photo and signature.

options.text: A library card
options.why: Wrong. Library cards are weak, non-government evidence.

options.text: A gym membership card
options.why: Wrong. Private and easy to obtain under any name.

options.text: A credit card
options.why: Wrong. Issued by a bank, usually without a photo.

explanation: Government-issued photo IDs such as passports and driver's licenses are the usual satisfactory evidence.
